evidence.snippet: 74 (90%) of 82 patients had a positive interferon score
evidence.explanation: 90% of AGS patients have a positive peripheral-blood interferon score, but 7/8 IFN-score-negative patients carried RNASEH2B mutations (27% of all RNASEH2B cases). This qualifies the canonical model by showing a substantial RNASEH2B subgroup lacking the blood IFN biomarker; the case-control design assayed whole-blood ISG expression only and did not test pathway dependence in nervous tissue, so it does not establish IFN-independent disease in the nervous system.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar defects after RNASEH2B inactivation are rescued by p53 but not cGAS deletion
evidence.explanation: In a mouse model with complete `Rnaseh2b` inactivation throughout neural progenitors, cerebellar defects are rescued by p53 deletion but not by cGAS deletion, establishing a p53/DNA-damage-driven neuropathology arm in that neural-null model. This qualifies — but does not by itself establish across hypomorphic human RNASEH2 AGS — that p53/DNA-damage signaling is the primary driver of RNASEH2-related neuropathology generally.

evidence.snippet: impact on neurological manifestations was limited and heterogeneous
evidence.explanation: Multicenter retrospective JAK1/2 inhibitor study (12 treated vs 20 untreated) shows that IFN blockade improves immunological and dermatological features but neurological benefit is limited and heterogeneous. This limited/heterogeneous response is compatible with an IFN-independent CNS injury component, but the retrospective, non-randomized design cannot distinguish that from prenatal or irreversible injury, treatment timing, or incomplete CNS target engagement by the drug. The authors themselves conclude the results "suggest that the pathogenetic complexity of AGS goes beyond the JAK-STAT pathway."

hypotheses/0.description: AGS-causing variants perturb enzymes and sensors that normally clear, edit, process, or recognize nucleic acids and histone-associated chromatin. open_questions/0.rationale: SAMHD1 was characterized first as a dNTPase and only later as a factor acting at stalled replication forks. The fork-processing route to cytosolic single-stranded DNA is demonstrated in SAMHD1-depleted human cell lines, not in patient tissue or in an animal model that develops AGS-like disease, and no study separates the two activities with function-selective SAMHD1 alleles in such a system. Until that is done, the proximal self-DNA species in SAMHD1-related AGS is unidentified, and treatments aimed at the DNA-sensing arm cannot be matched to a defined substrate for this genotype.

evidence.snippet: our study shows the safety of early initiation of therapy and supports the hope to slow renal failure by many years, emphasizing the value of preemptive therapy.

evidence.snippet: We now recommend the initiation of treatment at the time of diagnosis in males with X-linked Alport syndrome and in males and females with autosomal recessive Alport syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Updated clinical guidelines now recommend ACE inhibitor initiation at diagnosis for X-linked males and autosomal recessive patients.

treatments/0.description: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (e.g., ramipril, enalapril) are the cornerstone of treatment, shown to delay progression to ESRD by reducing proteinuria and glomerular hyperfiltration. evidence.snippet: While renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) blockade remains the foundation of treatment to delay kidney failure, it does not directly target the underlying molecular pathology.
evidence.explanation: Review confirms RAAS blockade (which includes both ACE inhibitors and ARBs) as the foundation of Alport syndrome treatment.

treatments/1.description: ARBs are used as an alternative or addition to ACE inhibitors for patients who cannot tolerate ACE inhibitors. RAAS blockade is the foundation of treatment for Alport syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Adjunctive commercially available metabolic modulators, including SGLT2i, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, ezetimibe and GLP-1 receptor agonists, may offer additional kidney protection.
evidence.explanation: Review identifies SGLT2 inhibitors as adjunctive therapy that may offer additional kidney protection beyond RAAS blockade, though evidence is emerging.

treatments/2.description: Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors may offer additional kidney protection as adjunctive therapy to RAAS blockade in adults with proteinuria and CKD. A pediatric RCT (DOUBLE PRO-TECT Alport, NCT05944016) is underway.

treatments/3.description: Dialysis (hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis) is required when patients progress to end-stage renal disease. This serves as a bridge to kidney transplantation.

evidence.snippet: De novo anti-GBM nephritis after transplantation was less frequent than previously reported, occurring in only 1.4% of AS patients, and in 2% of males with COL4A5 mutation.

evidence.snippet: Alport post-transplant nephritis (APTN) is an aggressive form of anti-glomerular basement membrane disease that targets the allograft in transplanted patients with X-linked Alport syndrome.

treatments/4.description: Kidney transplantation is the definitive treatment for ESRD in Alport syndrome. evidence.snippet: Hearing aids as needed for SNHL; cataract removal as needed

treatments/6.description: Anterior lenticonus and cataract can impair vision in Alport syndrome; cataract removal (lens extraction) is performed as needed for visually significant lens opacity.

evidence.snippet: Drink adequate fluids as dehydration may accelerate the progression of nephropathy.

treatments/7.description: Maintain adequate fluid intake; dehydration may accelerate progression of the nephropathy - a GeneReviews agents/circumstances-to-avoid recommendation.

evidence.snippet: Protection of corneas from minor trauma in those with recurrent corneal erosions.

treatments/8.description: Protect the corneas from minor trauma in patients with recurrent corneal erosions (an ocular manifestation of Alport syndrome) - a GeneReviews agents/circumstances-to-avoid recommendation.

treatments/9.description: Minimize exposure to loud noise to limit additional noise-induced hearing loss atop the sensorineural hearing loss - a GeneReviews agents/circumstances-to-avoid recommendation.

evidence.snippet: In females with XLAS and individuals with autosomal dominant Alport syndrome (ADAS), ESKD is frequently delayed until later adulthood, SNHL is relatively late in onset, and ocular involvement is rare.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents the delayed, variable course in XLAS females and ADAS, underscoring the unmet need for progression predictors.

open_questions/0.rationale: X-linked carrier females and autosomal dominant Alport syndrome show wide, poorly predictable variability in renal outcome - many reach ESKD only in later adulthood or not at all - so clinicians cannot reliably stratify risk or time nephroprotective therapy. Identifying predictive genotype (variant type/position, X-inactivation) and non-genetic modifiers would enable risk-adapted surveillance and treatment.

evidence.snippet: In SCA6 brains, numerous oval or rod-shaped aggregates were seen exclusively in the cytoplasm of Purkinje cells.

evidence.snippet: The pathogenesis of SCA6 is apparently linked to an age-dependent process accompanied by accumulation of mutant Ca(V)2.1 channels.
evidence.explanation: Knock-in data support age-dependent mutant Cav2.1 accumulation rather than a simple channel-density defect.

evidence.snippet: Novel activation of a store-operated calcium current due to ER stress is the cause for Purkinje neuron spiking abnormalities in SCA6 mice.
evidence.explanation: This supports ER-stress-linked membrane hyperexcitability in the current model.

steps/9.description: The SCA6 CAG expansion lengthens a polyglutamine tract in the C-terminal region encoded by CACNA1A. Mutant Cav2.1 accumulates in Purkinje cells and produces cytoplasmic aggregates. Current knock-in evidence supports misfolded-protein/ER stress, an initially protective HSP90-dependent unfolded-protein response, and age-related loss of that compensation, followed by store-operated calcium current and Purkinje-cell membrane hyperexcitability. The contribution of altered intrinsic Cav2.1 ion flux remains debated and is not modeled as a directional loss of calcium transport.

evidence.snippet: The yeast equivalent, P580H EF2, demonstrated impaired translocation, detected as an increased rate of -1 programmed ribosomal frameshift read-through in a dual-luciferase assay for observing translational recoding.
evidence.explanation: The functional assay directly supports impaired translational fidelity.

steps/10.description: In the original SCA26 pedigree, the segregating EEF2 p.Pro596His substitution affects a conserved domain required to maintain the reading frame during translation. The yeast-equivalent variant increases programmed -1 ribosomal frameshift read-through and sensitizes cells to unfolded-protein stress. Because evidence is centered on one family and functional model systems, this mechanism remains provisional pending independent human replication.

evidence.snippet: The repeat insertion was located in introns of TK2 and BEAN (brain expressed, associated with Nedd4) expressed in the brain and formed RNA foci in the nuclei of patients' Purkinje cells.
evidence.explanation: The original study demonstrates repeat-containing RNA foci in patient Purkinje cells.

steps/11.description: The pathogenic SCA31 insertion contains a long (TGGAA)n tract in an intron shared by oppositely transcribed BEAN1 and TK2. The BEAN1-direction (UGGAA)n transcript forms nuclear RNA foci in Purkinje cells, binds serine/arginine-rich splicing factors, and is toxic in cultured-cell systems, supporting repeat-RNA toxicity and disturbed RNA processing.

evidence.snippet: Arachidonic acid and docosahexaenoic acid, two final products of the enzyme, were reduced in the serum of affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: In transfection experiments, subcellular localization of altered ELOVL5 showed a perinuclear distribution with a signal increase in the Golgi compartment, whereas the wild-type showed a widespread signal in the endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence.explanation: Shows the mislocalization of the altered enzyme that accompanies the loss of elongation output.

evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemistry on control mice and human brain demonstrated high levels in Purkinje cells.
evidence.explanation: Supports binding the Purkinje cell on this node by showing where the enzyme is expressed in human and mouse brain.

steps/12.description: Missense ELOVL5 alleles impair the elongase step in omega-3 and omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acid synthesis. Carriers have reduced circulating arachidonic acid and docosahexaenoic acid, the enzyme's end products, and the altered protein redistributes from the endoplasmic reticulum towards the Golgi in transfected cells. The enzyme is present at high level in Purkinje cells, which is the basis for reading a systemic elongation defect as a Purkinje-cell vulnerability.

evidence.snippet: This is the first report of SCA41 caused by the c.1955A>G variant in the TRPC3 gene, which expands the mutation spectrum of the TRPC3 gene.

steps/13.description: Heterozygous TRPC3 missense variants are reported in two unrelated patients with cerebellar ataxia. TRPC3 is a non-selective cation channel of cerebellar signalling and mouse models of Trpc3 dysfunction are ataxic, but the functional consequence of the reported human alleles is not characterised in the sources cited here, so this node deliberately asserts no direction of change and carries no ontology-bound process. It exists so that the TRPC3 claim is visible in the graph at the confidence the literature supports and no higher.

evidence.snippet: These results indicate that mutant β-III spectrin causes mislocalization and dysfunction of mGluR1α at dendritic spines and connects SCA5 with other disorders involving glutamatergic dysfunction and synaptic plasticity abnormalities.

steps/17.description: FAT2 is an atypical cadherin selectively expressed in cerebellar granule cells, whose axons form the parallel fibres that synapse onto Purkinje cells. It binds Cbln1, a secreted organiser of Purkinje-cell synapse formation, and removing Fat2 in mice weakens parallel fibre synaptic strength and impairs motor behaviour. The node therefore places the FAT2 lesion at the granule cell to Purkinje cell synapse rather than inside the Purkinje cell itself.

steps/20.description: Dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor, and upper-limb incoordination accompany the gait syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The dominantly inherited spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA) are a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive gait ataxia, upper limb incoordination, and dysarthria.
evidence.explanation: Dysarthria is explicitly part of the SCA26 cerebellar phenotype.

steps/21.description: Cerebellar dysarthria commonly develops as the disorder progresses.

evidence.snippet: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 11 (SCA11) is characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia and abnormal eye signs (jerky pursuit, horizontal and vertical nystagmus).
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents horizontal and vertical nystagmus in SCA11.

steps/22.description: Gaze-evoked, horizontal, vertical, or downbeat nystagmus can accompany the cerebellar syndrome; its pattern and frequency vary by subtype.

evidence.snippet: Although not fatal, ADCA Type III may cause dysphagia and falls, which reduce the quality of life of the patients and may in turn shorten the lifespan.
evidence.explanation: The class review directly identifies dysphagia.

steps/23.description: Swallowing impairment can emerge during progression and contributes to nutritional, aspiration, and quality-of-life burden.

evidence.snippet: Although not fatal, ADCA Type III may cause dysphagia and falls, which reduce the quality of life of the patients and may in turn shorten the lifespan.
evidence.explanation: The class review directly identifies falls as a complication.

steps/24.description: Progressive gait instability can cause recurrent falls.

evidence.snippet: We have developed a mouse model to understand the mechanistic basis for this disease and show that expression of mutant but not wild-type β-III spectrin causes progressive motor deficits and cerebellar degeneration.
evidence.explanation: The SCA5 mouse model connects mutant spectrin to cerebellar degeneration.

edges/9.description: Postsynaptic receptor and transporter mislocalization impairs Purkinje-cell signaling and precedes progressive cerebellar degeneration.

evidence.snippet: Our studies support a model whereby proteotoxicity from misfolded mutant Cav2.1 is mitigated by a HSP90-dependent UPR, and age-related breakdown of this response causes motor dysfunction and aberrant Purkinje neuron spiking.
evidence.explanation: The current age-series model directly links proteotoxicity and UPR failure to Purkinje dysfunction.

edges/10.description: Age-dependent failure of proteostatic compensation permits aberrant Purkinje-cell firing and progressive motor dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: These studies provide a molecular foundation to understand the cellular and molecular pathogenesis of human SCA11, and help account for the link between ciliary dysfunction and neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence.explanation: The edge is partial because the study establishes the ciliary mechanism in models rather than the complete human degenerative chain.

edges/11.description: Ciliary assembly and signaling defects provide a model-supported route from truncated TTBK2 to Purkinje-neuron vulnerability.

evidence.snippet: Our results present a compelling candidate mutation and mechanism for the pathogenesis of SCA26 and further support the role of proteostatic disruption in neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence.explanation: The authors describe a compelling candidate rather than a multiply replicated human mechanism.

edges/12.description: Loss of translational fidelity and heightened proteostatic stress are the proposed intermediates linking the EEF2 variant to cerebellar degeneration.

evidence.snippet: Taking these findings together, we conclude that the RNA foci containing BEAN1-direction transcript (UGGAA)n are associated with PC degeneration in SCA31.
evidence.explanation: Human tissue and cell data connect repeat-RNA foci with Purkinje-cell degeneration.

edges/13.description: Toxic BEAN1-direction repeat RNA and nuclear foci are associated with Purkinje-cell degeneration.

evidence.snippet: The dominantly inherited spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA) are a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive gait ataxia, upper limb incoordination, and dysarthria.
evidence.explanation: The defining SCA26 report links the cerebellar disorder to progressive gait ataxia.

edges/14.description: Cerebellar cortical dysfunction impairs gait and stance coordination.

evidence.snippet: The dominantly inherited spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA) are a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive gait ataxia, upper limb incoordination, and dysarthria.
evidence.explanation: Upper-limb incoordination is a defining clinical consequence.

edges/15.description: Cerebellar cortical dysfunction impairs upper-limb coordination.

evidence.snippet: The dominantly inherited spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA) are a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive gait ataxia, upper limb incoordination, and dysarthria.
evidence.explanation: Dysarthria is part of the defining progressive cerebellar syndrome.

edges/16.description: Cerebellar dysfunction impairs timing and coordination of speech.

evidence.snippet: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 11 (SCA11) is characterized by progressive cerebellar ataxia and abnormal eye signs (jerky pursuit, horizontal and vertical nystagmus).
evidence.explanation: SCA11 directly demonstrates nystagmus within the ADCA-III class.

edges/17.description: Cerebellar oculomotor dysfunction produces gaze-evoked or other nystagmus.

evidence.snippet: Although not fatal, ADCA Type III may cause dysphagia and falls, which reduce the quality of life of the patients and may in turn shorten the lifespan.
evidence.explanation: The class review identifies dysphagia as a clinically important consequence.

edges/18.description: Progressive cerebellar and bulbar coordination deficits can impair swallowing.

evidence.snippet: Brain imaging documented cerebellar atrophy with sparing of cerebral cortex and no white matter disease.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the cerebellum-restricted atrophy that this edge asserts in SCA38 carriers.

edges/19.description: The elongation defect is read as a Purkinje-cell vulnerability because the enzyme is concentrated in those cells; SCA38 imaging shows cerebellar atrophy that spares the cerebral cortex.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, genetic mouse models of TRPC3 dysfunction display cerebellar ataxia, making the TRPC3 gene an excellent candidate for screening ataxic patients with unknown genetic aetiology.
evidence.explanation: The mouse evidence that TRPC3 dysfunction produces cerebellar ataxia; the sentence restates the established mouse models rather than this paper's own screen.

edges/20.description: The link from TRPC3 dysfunction to cerebellar degeneration rests on mouse models rather than on a characterised human allele, and is recorded at that strength.

evidence.snippet: This is consistent with the neuropathological examination, which showed severe Purkinje cell loss.
evidence.explanation: Human neuropathology in the CACNA1G family supports this edge.

edges/21.description: Neuropathology in a CACNA1G family showed severe Purkinje cell loss, linking the channel defect to the class-defining cerebellar degeneration.

evidence.snippet: SCA45/FAT2-associated late-onset cerebellar ataxia was reported in 2017 in 2 families with pure cerebellar syndrome with age of onset after 40 years of age. Similar few families with SCA45 have been reported so far.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the human pure cerebellar phenotype at the end of this edge; the sentence restates the 2017 report rather than this case report's own finding.

edges/22.description: Weakened parallel fibre input and disrupted Cbln1-dependent synapse organisation degrade Purkinje-cell function; in humans SCA45 presents as a pure cerebellar syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Although not fatal, ADCA Type III may cause dysphagia and falls, which reduce the quality of life of the patients and may in turn shorten the lifespan.
evidence.explanation: The review identifies falls as a consequence of the progressive syndrome.

edges/23.description: Progressive gait instability increases fall risk.

evidence.snippet: Ikeda et al. (2006) discovered that β-III spectrin (SPTBN2) mutations cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 5 (SCA5) in the American kindred and two additional independently reported SCA5 families.
evidence.explanation: This establishes the dominant SPTBN2-SCA5 association.

genes/0.notes: Dominant SPTBN2 variants alter beta-III spectrin and disrupt Purkinje-cell postsynaptic organization. Biallelic and de novo SPTBN2 disorders are distinct allelic conditions and should not be conflated with classic SCA5.

evidence.snippet: Genetically, SCA6 is caused by expansion of a trinucleotide CAG repeat in the last exon of longest isoform CACNA1A gene on chromosome 19p13.1-p13.2.
evidence.explanation: The review establishes the CACNA1A repeat-expansion cause.

genes/1.notes: The expansion lies in the final exon of CACNA1A and encodes a polyglutamine tract. Other CACNA1A variant classes cause overlapping but distinct channelopathies, including episodic ataxia type 2 and familial hemiplegic migraine type 1.

evidence.snippet: SCA11 is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the Serine/Threonine kinase Tau tubulin kinase 2 (TTBK2) that result in premature truncations of the protein.
evidence.explanation: This supports truncating TTBK2 variants as the cause of SCA11.

genes/2.notes: The best-supported functional model is mild dominant-negative interference by truncated TTBK2 rather than simple haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: We identified a single variant that co-segregates with the disease phenotype that produces a single amino acid substitution in eukaryotic elongation factor 2.
evidence.explanation: Cosegregation and functional data support EEF2, with single-family limitations.

genes/3.notes: The p.Pro596His variant was identified in the original SCA26 family and has functional support for translational infidelity and proteostatic stress. Because independent adult-onset SCA26 replication is limited, causal and mechanistic confidence is lower than for SCA5, SCA6, SCA11, or SCA31.

evidence.snippet: The other was an insertion, from 2.5-3.8 kb long, consisting of complex penta-nucleotide repeats including a long (TGGAA)n stretch.
evidence.explanation: The original study identifies the pathogenic SCA31 repeat insertion.

genes/4.notes: The insertion occupies overlapping intronic sequence in the oppositely transcribed BEAN1/TK2 region. BEAN1 is the structured gene anchor because the toxic repeat-containing transcript is produced in the BEAN1 direction.

evidence.snippet: We mapped SCA38 to a 56 Mb region on chromosome 6p in a SCA-affected Italian family by whole-genome linkage analysis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the chromosome 6p SCA38 locus by whole-genome linkage in the index family, the step that identified ELOVL5.

evidence.snippet: We extended our clinical and brain neuroimaging data on SCA38 including 21 cases from three Italian families. All had the ELOVL5 c.689G > T (p.Gly230Val) missense mutation.
evidence.explanation: Names the recurrent c.689G>T (p.Gly230Val) ELOVL5 allele carried by all 21 characterised cases.

evidence.snippet: ELOVL5 encodes an elongase involved in the synthesis of polyunsaturated fatty acids of the ω3 and ω6 series.
evidence.explanation: States the enzymatic role that makes this a fatty-acid metabolism ataxia.

genes/5.notes: A conventional missense mechanism rather than a repeat expansion. ELOVL5 is a fatty-acid elongase in the omega-3 and omega-6 polyunsaturated pathway, and the enzyme's downstream products are measurably reduced in carriers. The ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity download of 2026-09-25 contains no ELOVL5 assertion, so no validity classification is available for this relationship.

evidence.snippet: This is the first report of SCA41 caused by the c.1955A>G variant in the TRPC3 gene, which expands the mutation spectrum of the TRPC3 gene.
evidence.explanation: A second unrelated patient with a distinct TRPC3 missense allele.

evidence.snippet: The transient receptor potential (TRP) family member TRPC3 is a non-selective cation channel linked to key signalling pathways that are affected in cerebellar ataxia.
evidence.explanation: States what the TRPC3 product is and why it was a cerebellar-ataxia candidate. The sentence describes channel biology and names no experiment, in this paper or any other, so there is no study type for evidence_source to grade; the mouse evidence is cited separately on the downstream edge.

genes/6.notes: TRPC3 encodes a non-selective cation channel of Purkinje cell signalling. The human evidence is two unrelated single patients; mouse models of Trpc3 dysfunction are ataxic, which is why the gene was screened as a candidate in the first place.

evidence.snippet: In a large family affected by ADCA and mild pyramidal signs, we searched for the causative variant by combining linkage analysis and whole-exome sequencing.
evidence.explanation: The French linkage and exome study that identified CACNA1G in dominant cerebellar ataxia.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we analyzed a Japanese family with autosomal dominant SCA using linkage analysis and exome sequencing, and identified CACNA1G, which encodes the calcium channel CaV3.1, as a new causative gene.
evidence.explanation: Independent identification of the same gene in a Japanese family.

genes/7.notes: A conventional missense channelopathy of Cav3.1, the low-voltage-activated T-type calcium channel, not a repeat expansion. The recurrent p.Arg1715His substitution lies in the voltage sensor of repeat IV and shifts the channel's voltage dependence in the positive direction. ClinGen's Syndromic Disorders Gene Curation Expert Panel classified CACNA1G-SCA42 as Definitive on 2024-12-04 (assertion CGGV:assertion_b5e57bac-5985-4f39-a35e-ae2f3db0a5bf-2024-12-04T170000.000Z, read from the Gene-Disease Validity download of 2026-09-25) and lumped SCA42ND into SCA42 on the grounds that the molecular mechanism could not be distinguished between them.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report five novel spinocerebellar ataxia genes, FAT2, PLD3, KIF26B, EP300, and FAT1, identified through a combination of exome sequencing in genetically undiagnosed families and targeted resequencing of exome candidates in a cohort of singletons.
evidence.explanation: The report that establishes FAT2 as a dominant spinocerebellar ataxia gene.

genes/8.notes: FAT2 is an atypical cadherin selectively expressed in cerebellar granule cells. It was reported as a dominant ataxia gene in a 2017 exome and network study together with PLD3, KIF26B, EP300 and FAT1. The PLD3 claim from that paper drew published correspondence (Brain 2018;141:e78, with the authors' reply at e79), which is a reason to keep the confidence attached to FAT2 explicit rather than inherited from the paper's other genes. The ClinGen Gene-Disease Validity download of 2026-09-25 contains no FAT2 assertion.

evidence.snippet: Management is supportive; there are no known disease-modifying treatments to date.
evidence.explanation: Current SCA11 GeneReviews supports supportive rather than disease-modifying management.

evidence.snippet: Physiotherapy and assessment for assistive devices for ambulation; occupational therapy, including home adaptations; speech and language therapy for dysarthria and dysphagia
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies the multidisciplinary supportive interventions.

treatments/0.description: No established disease-modifying therapy exists for the canonical ADCA-III subtypes. Management uses physiotherapy for gait and balance, occupational therapy and home adaptation, speech and language therapy for dysarthria and dysphagia, and mobility or communication aids as needed. Subtype-specific experimental drugs should be represented as clinical trials rather than routine treatment.

evidence.snippet: These findings suggest the possibility that SCA6 is a channelopathy, and that the underlying mutation in SCA6 causes Purkinje cell degeneration through excessive entry of calcium ions.
evidence.explanation: This is the older channel-gain interpretation.

evidence.snippet: Neither voltage sensitivity of activation nor inactivation was altered in the Sca6(84Q) neurons, suggesting that expanded CAG repeat per se does not affect the intrinsic electrophysiological properties of the channels.
evidence.explanation: Native Purkinje-neuron data argue against a simple intrinsic channel-gating explanation.

evidence.snippet: The impairments in Purkinje neuron spiking are unrelated to Cav2.1 ion-flux function.
evidence.explanation: Current work explicitly separates membrane hyperexcitability from Cav2.1 ion flux.

open_questions/0.rationale: Xenopus-oocyte work suggested beta4-dependent enhanced channel activation and excessive calcium entry. Knock-in Purkinje-neuron recordings instead found unchanged current density and voltage dependence, and the 2026 age-series study attributed abnormal spiking to ER-stress-induced store-operated calcium current rather than Cav2.1 ion flux. The entry therefore represents proteotoxicity and ER-stress evidence without assigning a directional CACNA1A transport defect.

evidence.snippet: The responsible gene is yet to be determined, but ODZ3 is a plausible candidate.
evidence.explanation: The defining report explicitly records the unresolved causal gene.

open_questions/1.rationale: The phenotype and chromosome 4q34.3-q35.1 locus are defined in one family, but no causal variant has been established. ODZ3/TENM3 was nominated only as a candidate, so adding a SCA30 genetic or mechanism node would overstate the evidence.

evidence.snippet: Using whole-exome sequencing of three proband-parent trios, we identified de novo missense changes in the cytoplasmic actin-encoding genes ACTB and ACTG1 in one and two probands, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that de novo missense mutations in cytoplasmic actin genes ACTB and ACTG1 are the molecular cause of Baraitser-Winter syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Sequencing of both genes in 15 additional affected individuals identified disease-causing mutations in all probands, including two recurrent de novo alterations (ACTB, encoding p.Arg196His, and ACTG1, encoding p.Ser155Phe).
evidence.explanation: The founding study found an ACTB or ACTG1 missense variant in each of 18 selected probands; this is a cohort finding, not proof of universal de novo inheritance.

evidence.snippet: Several observations support a dominant-negative or gain-of-function mechanism for the disease-causing mutations.
evidence.explanation: The founding study supports an altered-function dominant mechanism rather than simple haploinsufficiency, without resolving one universal biochemical direction.

steps/2.description: Heterozygous ACTB or ACTG1 missense variants alter cytoplasmic actin function. Dominant-negative or gain-of-function effects are supported; a uniform increase in actin stability and simple haploinsufficiency are not established mechanisms for classic BRWS.

evidence.snippet: We detected similar expression levels between the mutant (p.S348L) ... while the signal of PFN1 was noticeably reduced in the sample with mutant ACTB (p.S348L)
evidence.explanation: Tsujimoto et al. (2024), Compromised actin dynamics underlie the orofacial cleft in Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome with a variant in ACTB: GFP pulldown from MDCK extracts mixed with exogenous PFN1 shows reduced association. This is not a measured binding constant.

steps/3.description: ACTB Ser348Leu shows reduced association with exogenous PFN1 in GFP-pulldown experiments from transfected MDCK cells. This allele-specific result suggests altered interactions with an actin-polymerization factor; an equilibrium affinity constant was not measured.

evidence.snippet: We observed an increased resistance to latrunculin A in β-actin p.Arg196His mutant cells, which is consistent with the previously reported p.Arg183Trp mutation34, whereas the γ-actin p.Ser155Phe mutant displayed increased sensitivity to the treatment
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived lymphoblastoid cells show opposite drug sensitivities for these two alleles; increased filament stability is not a uniform consequence of BRWS variants.

steps/4.description: Patient lymphoblastoid cells show mutation-specific F-actin accumulation and abnormal morphology. ACTB Arg196His confers relative latrunculin resistance whereas ACTG1 Ser155Phe increases sensitivity. Other variants and tissues can show different biochemical behavior; organoids do not show a corresponding uniform increase in actin abundance.

evidence.snippet: we observed a higher density of microtubule bundles at the apical cell cortex that appeared to be anchored to the apical adherens junction belt rather than being nucleated at the basal body of the primary cilium
evidence.explanation: Electron microscopy identifies abnormal apical cytoskeletal organization in the patient-derived organoids. The authors did not quantify these ultrastructural changes or establish their causal relation to spindle orientation.

steps/5.description: Patient-derived cerebral organoids show variable apical cell shape, intercellular protrusions, and increased apical microtubule bundles. The adherens-junction belt is largely preserved and astral microtubule counts are unchanged. These observations are candidate contributors to altered spindle positioning rather than proven individual causes.

evidence.snippet: We found that in contrast to the predominantly vertical cleavage plane orientation of mitotic APs in control cerebral organoids, mitotic APs of BWCFF-S cerebral organoids exhibited a nearly randomized or majoritarian horizontal cleavage plane orientation
evidence.explanation: This is the directly observed division-orientation phenotype in ACTB Thr120Ile and ACTG1 Thr203Met patient-derived organoids.

steps/6.description: ACTB Thr120Ile and ACTG1 Thr203Met patient-derived cerebral organoids show a shift away from predominantly vertical apical-progenitor cleavage planes. Engineered heterozygous ACTB Thr120Ile organoids reproduce this finding. Cleavage angle constrains possible division modes but does not by itself determine daughter-cell fate.

evidence.snippet: quantification of the DAPI-stained nuclei revealed a substantial decrease of the number of VZ progenitors per ventricle-like structure in the BWCFF-S organoids as compared to control organoids
evidence.explanation: Direct cell counting documents a smaller ventricular-zone progenitor pool; unchanged Ki-67 and PH3 proportions do not establish a general block in cell cycling.

steps/7.description: The organoid ventricular zone contains fewer progenitors per ventricle-like structure and is thinner. The basal-progenitor-to-radial-glia ratio is increased; greater basal progenitor production is inferred from these observations. Apoptotic cells remain rare and the proportions of Ki-67- and PH3-positive cells are not significantly different, so progenitor depletion should not be equated with a general cell-cycle arrest.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, the mutant ACTB (p.S348L) did not show an intense signal at the cell junction but rather showed uniform expression in the cytoplasm
evidence.explanation: This result is specifically from MDCK cells overexpressing GFP-tagged ACTB.

steps/8.description: Overexpressed ACTB Ser348Leu has reduced localization at epithelial cell junctions in MDCK cells and live Xenopus animal-cap epithelium. Diffuse mutant protein does not behave like endogenous filamentous actin during latrunculin treatment. Impaired incorporation is favored, but detailed polymerization effects remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: We observed that the mutant ACTB (p.S348L) -overexpressing cells displayed slower migration over time than the wild-type ACTB-overexpressing cells
evidence.explanation: The MDCK assay measures closure of a defined cell-free gap after removal of a silicone insert. It is a surrogate for epithelial behavior, not direct measurement of patient palatal fusion.

steps/9.description: MDCK cells overexpressing ACTB Ser348Leu close a defined cell-free gap more slowly than cells overexpressing wild-type ACTB. This experimental behavior supports a candidate epithelial contribution to clefting rather than a directly observed patient palatal-fusion defect.

evidence.snippet: Nearly all patients with ACTG1 mutations, and around 60% of those with ACTB mutations have some degree of pachygyria with anteroposterior severity gradient, rarely lissencephaly or neuronal heterotopia.
evidence.explanation: The cohort documents the anatomical cortical-malformation pattern. It does not directly measure neuronal migration, laminar connectivity, or the origin of the anteroposterior gradient.

evidence.snippet: Intellectual disability and epilepsy are variable in severity and largely correlate with CNS anomalies.
evidence.explanation: The association between neurological severity and CNS malformations supports a contribution of cortical pathology, without establishing a specific circuit mechanism or excluding disability with normal MRI.

steps/10.description: Human imaging shows anterior-predominant pachygyria, with less frequent lissencephaly, heterotopia, and corpus-callosum abnormalities. These findings are compatible with disturbed cortical development but do not directly demonstrate a specific neuronal migration, axonal wiring, or regional-timing mechanism. Some affected individuals have no detectable cortical malformation.

evidence.snippet: Nearly all patients with ACTG1 mutations, and around 60% of those with ACTB mutations have some degree of pachygyria with anteroposterior severity gradient, rarely lissencephaly or neuronal heterotopia.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies pachygyria frequency by subtype in 42 cases, establishing it as the primary cortical malformation with characteristic gradient.

steps/11.description: Pachygyria is often anterior predominant. The 2015 clinically ascertained cohort reported it in nearly all ACTG1 cases and approximately 60% of ACTB cases; these selected-cohort proportions should not be treated as invariant gene-specific penetrance.

evidence.snippet: Microcephaly (~50%) Microcephaly may be of prenatal onset, usually mild, but may be severe w/lissencephaly
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The chapter reports approximately half of affected individuals and explicitly includes prenatal onset.

steps/12.description: Microcephaly may be prenatal or develop postnatally. Severity varies, with severe cases accompanying lissencephaly; it is not exclusively a secondary postnatal process.

evidence.snippet: In children with normal brain structure, motor delay is common, but otherwise development is only mildly to moderately delayed. ID is usually mild. Rare individuals with normal intelligence have also been reported.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The phenotype is common but not obligatory; the combined developmental-delay/intellectual-disability percentage is not assigned to each component independently.

steps/13.description: Intellectual disability ranges from mild to profound. Structural brain abnormalities influence severity, but impairment also occurs with apparently normal brain structure; rare individuals have normal intelligence.

evidence.snippet: Epilepsy, of no specific type and of variable severity, is present in 50% of individuals, often in conjunction with structural cerebral anomalies.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The chapter supplies a patient frequency and explicitly variable severity.

steps/14.description: Epilepsy affects approximately half of reported individuals and varies in type and severity. Onset is age dependent, ranging from the first months of life into adulthood. Some seizures are difficult to control, but refractoriness is not universal.

evidence.snippet: Developmental delay (DD) / intellectual disability (ID) is highly variable: ... In children with normal brain structure, motor delay is common
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The chapter distinguishes developmental function from visible brain malformation; its combined DD/ID frequency does not establish an isolated global-delay denominator.

steps/15.description: Developmental delay varies markedly. Motor and language development may be delayed even when no cortical malformation is visible on imaging.

evidence.snippet: Uni- or bilateral ocular coloboma that may extend from the iris to the macula, sometimes with microphthalmia
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): This supports iris involvement without assigning the combined ocular-coloboma frequency to iris coloboma alone.

steps/16.description: Unilateral or bilateral iris coloboma may occur, sometimes extending into the posterior segment. The roughly 30% frequency for all ocular coloboma is not an iris-specific estimate.

evidence.snippet: Bilateral ptosis (90%) ... Highly arched eyebrows (90%)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The chapter gives a specific bilateral-ptosis frequency.

steps/17.description: Bilateral congenital non-myopathic ptosis is a characteristic feature and can require surgery. A specific levator-muscle or neural-crest mechanism has not been established by the clinical evidence.

evidence.snippet: Widely spaced eyes (95%) ... Bilateral ptosis (90%)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The frequency concerns widely spaced eyes directly.

steps/18.description: Widely spaced eyes are a highly frequent craniofacial manifestation.

evidence.snippet: Prominent metopic ridging or trigonocephaly (65%)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The source groups the two findings; their frequencies cannot be separated.

steps/19.description: Trigonocephaly and a prominent metopic ridge are related but distinct findings. The reported 65% combines both and is not a trigonocephaly-specific estimate.

evidence.snippet: hypertelorism, broad nose with large tip and prominent root, congenital non-myopathic ptosis, ridged metopic suture and arched eyebrows.
evidence.explanation: The cohort describes a broad nose and prominent root; the 2014 severe-case series explicitly describes a broad nasal bridge. No compound nose frequency is assigned to this individual feature.

evidence.snippet: broad nasal bridge, broad nasal tip and columella, anteverted nostrils
evidence.explanation: The severe-case series documents the bridge and tip separately.

steps/20.description: A broad nasal bridge may accompany a broad nose and large tip; these dimensions are recorded separately.

evidence.snippet: Moderate short stature (44%) ... Cardiovascular abnormality (38%)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The table assigns 44% specifically to moderate short stature.

steps/21.description: Moderate short stature is common, with variable prenatal growth.

evidence.snippet: Reduction of shoulder girdle muscle bulk and progressive joint stiffness is common. Early muscular involvement, occasionally with congenital arthrogryposis, may be present.
evidence.explanation: Verloes et al. identify shoulder girdle muscle reduction and joint stiffness as common features in 42 BRWS cases, with occasional arthrogryposis.

steps/22.description: Reduced shoulder-girdle muscle bulk and progressive muscle wasting occur in some individuals. Congenital muscle hypoplasia and later atrophy are not interchangeable, and the aggregate neuromuscular frequency is not a shoulder-specific estimate.

evidence.snippet: Sensorineural hearing loss of variable degree may be present and can be progressive and require hearing aids.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): This specifically supports sensorineural impairment and variable course, without importing frequencies from nonsyndromic ACTG1 deafness.

steps/23.description: Sensorineural hearing impairment may be progressive and require amplification. Conductive hearing loss also occurs, so the combined 35% hearing-loss frequency is not applied to this subtype.

evidence.snippet: Moderate short stature (44%) ... Cardiovascular abnormality (38%)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The chapter reports 38% cardiovascular abnormality; the 2015 cohort independently reports congenital heart defects in 12 of 36 evaluated patients.

steps/24.description: Congenital cardiac malformations include septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, and valve abnormalities.

evidence.snippet: Structural renal malformation (10%) ... Micropenis, cryptorchidism, & hypospadias (rare)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The table distinguishes structural renal malformations from the broader genitourinary category.

steps/25.description: Structural renal anomalies include horseshoe or ectopic kidneys and duplication. Hydronephrosis is recorded separately.

evidence.snippet: Gastrointestinal dysfunction (41%) ... Frequent chronic constipation (requiring daily medication) & reflux disease
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The frequency applies to the broad gastrointestinal spectrum, not to every component.

steps/26.description: Gastrointestinal manifestations include constipation, reflux, feeding difficulties and occasional structural anomalies, with different mechanisms and management needs.

evidence.snippet: Iris and retinal coloboma and microphthalmia may severely impair vision.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The posterior-segment finding is distinct from iris coloboma.

steps/27.description: Retinal coloboma varies in extent; visual prognosis depends partly on macular and optic-disc involvement.

evidence.snippet: Uni- or bilateral ocular coloboma that may extend from the iris to the macula, sometimes with microphthalmia
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): This documents a distinct eye-size abnormality.

evidence.snippet: Bilateral ptosis (90%) ... Highly arched eyebrows (90%)
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews, Baraitser-Winter Cerebrofrontofacial Syndrome (March 2022 revision): The table estimates this feature at 90%.

steps/29.description: Highly arched eyebrows are a characteristic facial feature.

evidence.snippet: Prominent metopic ridging or trigonocephaly (65%)

steps/6.description: At the human ADD3 susceptibility locus, H69 cholangiocyte reporter assays detect allele-dependent activity in four fragments: risk haplotypes increase activity at E2, E4 and E10 but decrease it at E9. The fragment containing lead marker rs17095355 has no significant allelic difference. These assays concern cloned regulatory elements; they do not establish endogenous expression changes, a causal nucleotide, or chromatin contacts in patient cholangiocytes. The molecular-function annotation identifies the linked protein’s normal activity; it does not establish the functional effect of each human susceptibility allele.

steps/7.description: Gpc1 or add3a knockdown increases Hedgehog-pathway readouts in zebrafish. Cyclopamine partially rescues the associated biliary defects, supporting a model-specific contribution of excessive signaling. A uniform Hedgehog abnormality caused by each human susceptibility allele has not been demonstrated. The molecular-function annotation identifies the linked protein’s normal activity; it does not establish the functional effect of each human susceptibility allele.

The molecular-function annotation identifies the linked protein’s normal activity; it does not establish the functional effect of each human susceptibility allele.

Glutathione depletion sensitizes biliary cells, whereas NAC supplementation or Nrf2 activation reduces injury. This is a toxin-model mechanism; intrinsic glutathione deficiency has not been established as a general initiating human defect.

evidence.snippet: Patients with BA had decreased peripheral blood Treg frequency and lack of cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 (CTLA-4) upregulation despite a highly activated, effector Treg phenotype.

steps/10.description: Human BA samples show reduced Treg frequency and inadequate CTLA-4 upregulation, including blood collected at transplantation; these observations do not establish an initiating neonatal defect. evidence.snippet: Even though the percentage of T-bet KO mice displaying symptoms of an obstructive cholangiopathy and overall mortality rate was not different compared to wild-type mice, the extrahepatic bile ducts of T-bet KO mice remained patent.

steps/11.description: T-bet-dependent inflammatory and cytotoxic programs contribute to duct injury in the RRV mouse model. T-bet deletion reduces these programs and preserves duct patency in many mice, but cholestatic symptoms and mortality persist. Duct patency therefore does not establish complete disease rescue.

evidence.snippet: Targeted depletion of CD11c+ dendritic cells diminished hepatic IL-17A production and ameliorated intrahepatic bile duct injury.
evidence.explanation: Dendritic-cell perturbation in the RRV model.

evidence.snippet: Hepatic CD4+ lymphocytes were chief producers of IL-17A in patients with progressive disease undergoing liver transplantation.
evidence.explanation: Cellular cytokine-production finding in human clinical samples.

steps/12.description: In the post-obstructive phase of RRV-induced disease, dendritic cells promote Th17 responses. Depletion decreases hepatic IL-17A and intrahepatic injury without preventing the initial extrahepatic obstruction. Human IL-17A-positive-cell and macrophage associations support relevance but do not constitute equivalent intervention evidence.

evidence.snippet: Recombinant IL-17A induced expression of chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 2 in neonatal cholangiocytes in vitro
evidence.explanation: Direct cell-culture response to IL-17A.

steps/13.description: IL-17A induces CCL2 expression in cultured neonatal cholangiocytes. In this assay it does not directly kill the biliary cells; the proposed injury pathway involves recruitment of inflammatory cells.

evidence.snippet: blockade of the corresponding chemokine (C-C motif) receptor 2 reduced recruitment of inflammatory macrophages to the liver in vivo.
evidence.explanation: In vivo perturbation of the recruitment pathway.

evidence.snippet: the prevalence of IL-17A+ cells was positively correlated with the degree of CD68+ macrophage infiltration at diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: Human tissue association, not a test of CCR2 blockade.

steps/14.description: CCL2/CCR2 signaling recruits inflammatory Ly6C-high macrophages during later RRV-model injury. CCR2 blockade reduces recruitment, and disrupted IL-17 signaling preserves intrahepatic ducts and improves survival. In human tissue, IL-17A-positive cells correlate with CD68-positive infiltration; causal human intervention evidence is lacking.

evidence.snippet: addition of anti-Mip2/Cxcl2 antibodies depleted this chemokine in the conditioned media and completely prevented neutrophil chemotaxis.
evidence.explanation: Conditioned-medium depletion experiment; the causal intervention is in vitro.

steps/15.description: RRV-infected RAW264.7 macrophage conditioned medium recruits neutrophils, and CXCL2/Mip2 depletion abolishes this response. RRV is detected in hepatic macrophages in vivo, but the necessity of this chemotactic pathway for duct injury in vivo was not demonstrated. Infected cholangiocyte conditioned medium did not reproduce the response.

evidence.snippet: the RRV-infected Ig-α(-/-) mice did not have hyperbilirubinemia or bile duct obstruction.
evidence.explanation: Genetic B-cell deficiency protects against model pathology.

steps/16.description: B-cell-deficient mice resist RRV-induced biliary obstruction and have reduced Th1 inflammation. Treg depletion does not abolish this protection. Antigen presentation is a proposed explanation; this experiment does not establish that autoantibodies themselves cause human disease.

evidence.snippet: Cd177-/- BALB/c mice exhibited delayed disease onset and reduced morbidity and mortality.
evidence.explanation: Mouse genetic intervention.

evidence.snippet: these cells were associated with increased levels of reactive oxygen species and increased NET formation, which induced the apoptosis of biliary epithelial cells in cocultures.
evidence.explanation: The epithelial injury assay is in coculture, distinct from the in vivo mouse outcome.

steps/17.description: CD177-positive neutrophils in the RRV model exhibit increased oxidative activity and NET formation; coculture experiments link NET-associated activity to biliary epithelial apoptosis. Cd177 loss reduces experimental disease severity. Human NAC pilot observations are exploratory and do not establish durable clinical benefit. The 2025 corrigendum corrects duplicated representative flow plots, with the authors reporting unchanged underlying statistics.

evidence.snippet: the amount of cholangiocyte epithelial damage and bile duct edema was significantly greater in the early infection group
evidence.explanation: Histologic epithelial injury in the time-dependent RRV mouse model.

evidence.snippet: Biliatresone has selective toxicity for extrahepatic cholangiocytes (EHCs) in zebrafish larvae.
evidence.explanation: The plant toxin biliatresone selectively injures extrahepatic cholangiocytes, demonstrating that a targeted cholangiocyte insult can initiate a BA-like extrahepatic cholangiopathy.

steps/18.description: Cholangiocyte epithelial damage is a central lesion. RRV infection and biliatresone exposure produce experimentally defined injury in mice and zebrafish, respectively; neither demonstrates the initiating cause in human disease. Immune attack and developmental susceptibility may contribute through distinct, incompletely resolved routes.

evidence.snippet: Mild lymphocytic inflammation is usually present within portal tracts in BA. Other inflammatory cells, including eosinophils, plasma cells and macrophages, are also present.
evidence.explanation: Human pathology synthesis describes mixed portal inflammation.

evidence.snippet: Immune subpopulations inhabiting the 'fibrotic niche' (areas of scarring), comprising 'intermediate' CD14++ CD16+ monocytes, scar-associated macrophages, natural killer T cells, transitional B cells and FCN3+ neutrophils were identified.
evidence.explanation: Spatial association of immune populations with scar tissue, not a causal intervention.

steps/19.description: Periductal innate and adaptive immune activation accompanies biliary epithelial injury. Human tissue studies show inflammatory infiltrates and regulatory abnormalities; perturbation studies in neonatal RRV mice support contributions from Th1, Th17, B-cell and macrophage pathways. No single experimental immune mechanism establishes the cause of all human cases.

evidence.snippet: The transformation and proliferation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) from fat-storing cells to myofibroblasts in BA plays an important role in hepatic fibrogenesis. HSCs are responsible for increased extracellular matrix, which leads to progressive scarring
evidence.explanation: The pathology review supports mesenchymal activation and matrix production in biliary atresia.

steps/20.description: Sustained inflammation activates portal fibroblasts and transdifferentiates hepatic stellate cells into a myofibroblast-like, matrix-secreting phenotype — the organ-specific mesenchymal activation step of the conserved fibrotic response in the biliary atresia portal tract.

evidence.snippet: Histopathological findings in liver biopsies include the expansion of the portal tracts, with edematous fibroplasia and bile ductular proliferation, with bile plugs in duct lumen.
evidence.explanation: Portal-tract fibroplasia and ductular reaction on biopsy evidence the fibro-obliterative remodeling of this node.

evidence.snippet: The destructive fibroinflammatory process that underlies BA, may involve a short segment of a duct, an entire duct or the entire biliary system.
evidence.explanation: Fibroinflammatory remodeling of the resected biliary tree.

steps/21.description: Activated portal myofibroblasts deposit excess extracellular matrix around and within the injured ducts, producing a fibro-obliterative process that progressively narrows and obliterates the extrahepatic biliary tree and damages the intrahepatic ducts, forming the characteristic fibrous remnant at the porta hepatis. This obliteration is the anatomic substrate that the Kasai portoenterostomy attempts to bypass.

evidence.snippet: As this biliary timeline is shared by the determination of visceral situs, spleen formation, evolution of the portal venous and caval venous system anomalies it is not too much to speculate that BASM is also an embryonic defect.
evidence.explanation: Developmental interpretation of the BASM phenotype, not a proven single molecular cause.

evidence.snippet: The heterozygous transition c.433G>A (Ala145Thr) located in exon 5 was identified in 5 patients, with a twice-higher frequency than in control patients.
evidence.explanation: Small candidate-gene study; no Mendelian penetrance inference.

steps/22.description: The combination of biliary atresia with splenic, visceral-situs, vascular and cardiac malformations suggests disturbed embryonic patterning in BASM. CFC1, a NODAL coreceptor, and PKD1L1 are candidate links to left-right signaling in a subset, with supportive animal data; the underlying defect remains unresolved in most patients. The molecular-function annotation identifies the linked protein’s normal activity; it does not establish the functional effect of each human susceptibility allele.

evidence.snippet: Knockdown of gpc1 in zebrafish led to developmental biliary defects.
evidence.explanation: Experimental biliary developmental phenotype.

evidence.snippet: These data highlight the essential role of pkd1l1 in normal development and function of the zebrafish biliary system
evidence.explanation: Fish loss-of-function data support developmental plausibility rather than variant-specific human causality.

steps/23.description: Susceptibility-gene perturbations can impair developing biliary networks. Gpc1, add3a, arf6 and pkd1l1 studies provide distinct experimental routes, but sparse fish ducts are not equivalent to the human fibro-obliterated extrahepatic remnant. The molecular-function annotation identifies the linked protein’s normal activity; it does not establish the functional effect of each human susceptibility allele.

evidence.snippet: in adult Efemp1 +/- mouse ducts, elastin organization into fibers is decreased by approximately half.
evidence.explanation: Mouse matrix-organization phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Pressure myography showed that Efemp1 +/- ducts have altered mechanics compared to control ducts
evidence.explanation: Measured duct mechanics following heterozygous gene loss.

steps/24.description: Adult Efemp1 heterozygous mouse ducts have fewer organized elastic fibers despite preserved total elastin, with altered responses to pressure. This suggests structural susceptibility involving fibulin-3, but neither spontaneous atresia nor the direction of effect of human EFEMP1 risk variants was established. A mechanical contribution to epithelial vulnerability remains a hypothesis without a demonstrated causal edge to injury. The molecular-function annotation identifies the linked protein’s normal activity; it does not establish the functional effect of each human susceptibility allele.

evidence.snippet: Portal tracts show expansion and demonstrate edematous fibroplasia with bile ductular proliferation
evidence.explanation: Histologic epithelial expansion.

evidence.snippet: the reprogrammed cells expressed both hepatocyte and cholangiocyte markers.
evidence.explanation: Human tissue-derived single-cell coexpression.

evidence.snippet: Pseudotime analysis depicted a differentiation trajectory from hepatocytes across reprogrammed cells to cholangiocytes in BA.
evidence.explanation: Computational trajectory inference; not direct observation of human cell fate conversion.

steps/25.description: Expanded portal biliary epithelium is a characteristic tissue response. A 2025 human single-cell study found cells coexpressing hepatocyte and cholangiocyte markers; RNA velocity and pseudotime inferred a hepatocyte-to-biliary trajectory. These computational trajectories are not lineage tracing, and their downstream fibrogenic function remains partly inferential.

evidence.snippet: Patients who have undergone a Kasai portoenterostomy procedure are at risk of ascending cholangitis due to the resulting abnormal biliary anatomy.
evidence.explanation: Clinical review explicitly relates altered anatomy to postoperative cholangitis.

steps/26.description: The altered biliary-enteric anatomy after Kasai permits ascending infection of the remaining ducts. This secondary treatment-associated complication is distinct from hypotheses about the initiating cause of biliary atresia.

evidence.snippet: Biliary atresia is a progressive fibrosing obstructive cholangiopathy of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary system, resulting in obstruction of bile flow and neonatal jaundice.
evidence.explanation: Obstructive bile-flow impairment and neonatal jaundice, distinct from subsequent cirrhotic remodeling.

steps/27.description: Obstruction of the biliary tree reduces delivery of bile to the intestine and retains conjugated bilirubin and bile acids. Drainage may remain impaired after Kasai, while ongoing intrahepatic disease contributes to later liver injury.

evidence.snippet: Biliary pattern cirrhosis with irregular nodules are observed on microscopy.
evidence.explanation: Architectural endpoint seen in explanted livers.

steps/28.description: Persistent biliary injury and matrix deposition distort liver architecture into irregular regenerative nodules and scarring. Progression can continue despite restored extrahepatic drainage.

evidence.snippet: Higher stages of portal fibrosis have been associated with more severe portal hypertension and increased risk of LT
evidence.explanation: Disease-specific clinical-pathologic association.

steps/29.description: Fibrotic and cirrhotic remodeling increases resistance to portal flow, producing portal hypertension and its splenic, variceal and fluid-retention complications.

evidence.snippet: Patients with cholestatic conditions are at increased risk of malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins, like vitamin K.
evidence.explanation: Cholestatic malabsorption in the BA care guideline.

steps/30.description: Reduced intestinal bile delivery impairs fat and fat-soluble-vitamin absorption. Nutritional deficiency and increased metabolic demands contribute to poor growth; vitamin K depletion may impair hemostasis.

evidence.snippet: Biliary atresia (BA) and choledochal cysts are known to cause obstructive jaundice, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia will be observed.

steps/31.description: Elevation of the direct (conjugated) bilirubin fraction due to obstructed bile flow; the biochemical hallmark of neonatal cholestasis and the finding that mandates urgent evaluation for biliary atresia.

steps/32.description: Jaundice persisting beyond the first two weeks of life. In biliary atresia the jaundice is cholestatic (conjugated) rather than the benign unconjugated physiologic jaundice of the newborn.
